content.text: Distance-time graphs are a powerful way to visualise motion. By plotting distance against time, we can see at a glance how an object moves, whether it's stationary, moving at constant speed, or accelerating. Learning to interpret these graphs is an essential skill in physics.
On a distance-time graph, the gradient (slope) of the line equals the speed. Steeper = faster. Horizontal = stationary. A curve means the speed is changing (acceleration or deceleration).

Distance-time graphs help visualise journeys, including stops and different speeds.
GPS data can be plotted as distance-time graphs to analyse vehicle movements.
Split times in races can be plotted to analyse a runner's pacing strategy.
Motion sensors (data loggers) automatically produce distance-time graphs in the laboratory.

A common error is thinking a distance-time graph can slope downward. Since distance is always positive and can only increase or stay the same, the line on a distance-time graph never goes down. (A displacement-time graph, however, can go down.)
— On a distance-time graph, lines never go down. Distance can only increase or stay the same. (Displacement-time graphs CAN go down.)
— Steeper means faster, not higher. A steep line at a low position means fast speed but short total distance.
— A curved line means changing speed, not curved path.
— Horizontal means stationary, which is correct—but students sometimes confuse this with "moving at constant speed."
— You can only read speed (gradient). Acceleration requires a velocity-time graph or calculation from speed changes.
